The Galle Dutch Fort (also known simply as Galle Fort or the Ramparts of Galle) is a magnificent historical and archaeological monument located on the southwest coast of Sri Lanka. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site recognized for being the best example of a fortified city built by Europeans in South and Southeast Asia, showcasing a unique blend of European architecture and South Asian traditions.

Portugalilais-Hollantilais-Englantilainen linnoitus. Edellämainitut maat ovat jokainen tuoneet oman vivahduksen rakennuksien tyyliin, pieneen linnoituksen  " sisäänleivottuun " kaupunkiin. Tuhannet turistit pörräävät nähtävyydellä, mutta sekaan mahtuu kyllä hyvin. Näkemisen arvoinen linnoitus -Portuguese-Dutch-English fortress. The aforementioned countries have each brought their own touch to the style of the buildings, to the small fortress "baked in" the city. Thousands of tourists flock to the attraction, but there is plenty of room. A fortress worth seeing

All tourists enter the fort through the Main Gate. Built in 1873 by the British, they are a century younger than the Dutch ones.  The old gate is located behind the bastion of the Sun. They bear the Dutch abbreviation VOC (Vereinigte Oostindische Compagnie), the East India Company of the United Provinces, and a shield with the company's symbols - two lions and a rooster and the date 1669. The rooster (Gallo), which gave the name to the fort and the city, was inherited from the Portuguese, because they began building the fort back in 1588, limiting themselves to a wall from the land, because The Sinhalese kingdoms of Kotte and Kandy did not have a fleet, and they could not be afraid of attacks from the sea. The walls from the land (the bastion of the Moon with a Clock tower and the bastion of the Sun) are more powerful than from the sea. The Dutch had already built walls from the sea since 1649, rightly reasoning that it was not so much the local population that should be feared as colonizers from Europe. Just like them. The fears were not unfounded, and the fort was captured by the British in 1796, taking advantage of the occupation of the Netherlands by the French in 1795. At the same time, the fort, which had been fortified for so long, did not fire a single shot. The bastion at the old gate is the oldest.  It was built by the Portuguese, but its name is Dutch - Zwart.  Those who know German can guess by the consonance that it is "black".  Previously, the remains of the 17th-century Dutch ship Avondster, which sank nearby, were nearby, but they were washed out to sea in the terrible summer of 2004. The fort's 15 bastions, by the way, withstood the impact of the deadliest tsunami in history, which claimed the lives of almost 300,000 people in coastal countries. This proves once again in hindsight the level of the Dutch school of fortification. South of Zwart stands the Ackersloot bastion, erected shortly before the British captured it in 1789 and named after the birthplace of Captain Coster, who captured Halle in 1640. The eastern wall ends with the Utrecht bastion, also named after the famous Dutch city, the birthplace of football player Marco van Basten and erotic star Sylvia Kristel ("Emmanuel") (joke). There is a lighthouse built in 1938 on the cape nearby. Previously, before the lighthouse, signalmen from the Flag Rock bastion warned ships about the danger of rocks. In case of fog, the signal was given by the Musketeers. They shot from the nearest Pigeon Island, which could be reached from the fort at low tide. The inhabitants of the Netherlands could not do without their favorite wind turbines.  They installed it on the Triton bastion on the eastern wall. This is done specifically in the direction of the prevailing wind direction. The blades of the windmill rotated the gears of a pump that lifted seawater up. The Dutch watered the streets with it. But for sewage, the Dutch used the energy of the tides. At high tide, the water entered the network, and at low tide, it washed the feces into the sea. The old system is still working, so swimming near the fort is not recommended.

Galle Fort is one of the most enjoyable places to explore in southern Sri Lanka. The streets are lively and sounding are beautifully maintained, the architecture is a mix of Dutch and British influence, and the entire area has a relaxed coastal atmosphere. Walking along the ramparts at sunset is a highlight, and there are plenty of great spots for photography. from the lighthouse to the narrow alleyways and restored buildings. It’s easy to spend a few hours here enjoying cafés, small shops, and the views across the bay. A must-visit when travelling through the south. Although credit goes to Dutch for the Fort, there is Portuguese presence throughout the mega structure. This is well presented with clear information boards. The highlight for me was the Galle Maritime Museum. Well presented artifacts and presentations. I must do in Galle for Marine enthusiasts like my self. Ice cream from Gelato was as  memorable as the Poke lunch we had there.

Great restaurants and coffee places inside with lovely jewellery stores. Plenty to see and explore.

Galle Fort is a historic UNESCO-listed landmark on Sri Lanka’s south coast, blending colonial architecture, cobblestone lanes, and ocean views. Its charming cafés, boutiques, ramparts, and sunset points create a relaxed atmosphere. Visitors can explore museums, old churches, and vibrant streets that reflect a mix of Portuguese, Dutch, and British heritage.

A steady rain hammered the ancient, UNESCO-listed streets of Galle Fort as we ventured out, a lone umbrella our only shield against the tropical downpour. The cobblestones gleamed black under the deluge. Every few minutes, a persistent Tuk Tuk driver would whir up beside us, undeterred by our soaked state, and pitch a tour. "No, thank you!" we'd laugh, pushing on. We found a brief respite atop the massive fort wall, the wind whipping our clothes and the umbrella turned upside down as we watched the grey ocean churn below. The weather meant we couldn't complete the full circuit of the twelve historic bastions, but we did lose ourselves in the musty cool of the Historical Mansion Museum. Inside, forgotten relics of the colonial past—old appliances, housewares, photographs and heavy teak furniture—told silent stories. The best part? Entry didn't cost a cent. Afterwards, we meandered through a maze of gift shops, a perfect diversion for a wet morning.

Dutch landed to Galle in 1505 but stayed just few days. Later in 1518 they came again and build Galle Fort and ruled until English forces defeated them. In 1540 they build their Bastian here. At the time Fort was just a bear land. However, there was a natural Harbor which was active. In 1344 Iban Battuta landed here. It proves that there was an active harbor at that time. Also, three sides of this area were covered by sea and only one side have the access from land. So, they observed it is very secured place for them to build their Bastian. Another important reason to decide to build the Bastian here was that it is in the Silk Route and very convenient for commercial purpose. There are so many things with historical value in Galle Fort. It is one of the Most Popular destinations among Tourists.

Galle Fort is a fascinating blend of history, culture, and natural beauty that takes you on an unforgettable journey to the past. Situated on a scenic headland in southern Sri Lanka, this UNESCO World Heritage site is a perfect spot for history buffs and nature lovers alike. The Dutch Fort, with its well-preserved walls and remarkable ramparts, stands tall, offering breathtaking views of the ocean on three sides. It’s not just the views that make it special, but the ambiance of the place—the quiet streets, vibrant colonial architecture, and the sense of stepping back in time to the days of ancient trade routes. What I found most captivating was the rich history that surrounds the Fort. Did you know that this city is believed to have once traded with King Solomon, the Egyptians, and the Persians? That’s what makes a visit here so much more than just a stroll through old buildings—it’s a deep dive into Sri Lanka’s fascinating past. Take a leisurely walk along the fortifications, explore the various boutique shops, and enjoy the peaceful sunsets over the sea. It’s the perfect combination of history and natural beauty, ideal for anyone looking to explore the true essence of Galle. Pro Tips: Wear comfortable shoes as you’ll want to explore every corner of the Fort. The sunset views from the ramparts are something you don’t want to miss! Stop by the cozy cafes inside the Fort to enjoy some sea food. If you’re in Sri Lanka, Galle Fort is an absolute must-visit for its rich cultural heritage and stunning views. Whether you’re a solo traveler, couple, or family, you’ll find something to enjoy here. Highly recommended!

Galle Dutch Fort, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, stands as one of Sri Lanka’s most iconic landmarks, seamlessly blending colonial history, cultural heritage, and modern sophistication. My recent visit to this architectural marvel was nothing short of spectacular, offering a unique experience of walking through centuries-old cobblestone streets while indulging in modern luxuries. A Walk Through History Originally built by the Portuguese in 1588 and later fortified by the Dutch in the 17th century, Galle Fort has withstood the test of time, including tsunamis, wars, and changing civilizations. As I stepped inside the fort, I could feel the echoes of its colonial past—massive stone walls, ancient churches, and Dutch-style buildings standing resiliently against the backdrop of the Indian Ocean. One of the most fascinating aspects of Galle Fort is how history coexists with modernity. While some ruins tell tales of the past—like the crumbling bastions and weathered old warehouses—many colonial-era buildings have been beautifully restored and converted into boutique hotels, cafés, art galleries, and luxury shops. Modern Elegance Amidst Ruins Despite being a centuries-old structure, Galle Fort has evolved into a vibrant, upscale destination. The streets are lined with stylish cafés, high-end boutiques, chic restaurants, and boutique hotels, giving it a European-inspired coastal town vibe. It’s a rare sight where you find luxury brands, artisanal ice cream shops, and handcrafted jewelry stores sitting inside historic Dutch-era buildings! While it has become modernized and somewhat commercialized, it hasn’t lost its old-world charm. The fort still preserves its ancient ramparts, lighthouses, old trading posts, and stone-paved alleyways, making it a unique destination where the past meets the present. Must-Visit Spots in Galle Fort 1. Galle Lighthouse One of the most picturesque and Instagram-worthy spots in the fort, this 19th-century lighthouse offers breathtaking views of the Indian Ocean. It’s a perfect spot to catch a golden sunset or simply enjoy the sea breeze. 2. The Dutch Hospital Shopping Precinct A beautifully restored colonial-era hospital that has now been transformed into a modern shopping and dining hub. This area is perfect for those looking to enjoy fine dining, sip cocktails, or shop for unique souvenirs. 3. The Ramparts & Bastions Walking along the fort’s ancient walls is an experience in itself. These massive stone fortifications once protected the fort from invasions and now serve as a stunning viewpoint for both history lovers and photographers. Sunsets here are absolutely magical! 4. Historical Churches & Museums • Dutch Reformed Church (Groote Kerk): Built in 1755, this church is one of the oldest Protestant churches in Sri Lanka. • National Maritime Museum: Showcases artifacts from shipwrecks and colonial-era maritime history. • All Saints’ Church: A gorgeous Anglican church with intricate architecture and serene surroundings. 5. Flag Rock & Sunset Point At the far end of the fort lies Flag Rock, an old Portuguese watchtower that has now become a popular cliff-jumping and sunset-viewing spot. Watching the waves crash against the rocks while the sun dips below the horizon is an unforgettable experience. 6. The Quirky Streets & Hidden Alleys One of the best things to do in Galle Fort is to simply wander through its narrow, maze-like streets, each filled with hidden gems—antique shops, quirky cafés, street art, and local handicrafts. The vibe here is laid-back yet lively, perfect for leisurely exploration. The Food Scene – A Gastronomic Delight! Galle Fort has become a foodie’s paradise, offering everything from Sri Lankan seafood specialties to international fine dining. Some must-visit spots include: • Pedlar’s Inn Café – A cozy café serving excellent Sri Lankan rice & curry, coffee, and fresh seafood. • A Minute by Tuk Tuk – Located inside the Dutch Hospital, offering stunning ocean views with delicious seafood. • Isle of Gelato – The best place to grab some natural, handcrafted gelato to cool off after a day of exploring. Final Thoughts – Why Galle Fort is a Must-Visit! ⭐ A perfect mix of history, culture, and modern luxury ⭐ Breathtaking ocean views and stunning sunsets ⭐ Instagram-worthy colonial architecture and charming streets ⭐ A haven for foodies, shopaholics, and history lovers alike ⭐ A unique blend of ancient ruins and trendy lifestyle spots Whether you’re a history enthusiast, a photographer, a foodie, or just someone looking for a relaxing getaway, Galle Dutch Fort has something for everyone. It’s a place where you can sip coffee in a 300-year-old building, walk along 17th-century ramparts, and shop for designer clothes—all in one day!

The Galle Fort is the largest remaining fortress in Asia constructed by any European imperial powers. Also known as Dutch Fort or Ramparts of Galle, this architectural and archaeological wonder was first built in 1588 by the Portuguese and lavishly rebuilt by the Dutch during the 17th century. Even after long years from the construction, Galle Fort, a UNESCO's World Heritage Site, is still maintained as fresh. Galle is a major coastal town in the southwest of Sri Lanka and is the finest instance of a fortified city constructed by the Portuguese in Southeast Asia.

Walking Tour Experience A guided walking tour within Galle Fort is highly recommended. The guides, often locals, will share stories about the fort’s history, including the eras of Portuguese, Dutch, and British control, as well as insight into Sri Lanka’s colonial past and maritime heritage. The tour often includes stops at lesser-known sites like the All Saints’ Church, Amangalla Hotel (a historic colonial-era building), and the old Dutch government house.

The fort dates to 1588, constructed by the Portuguese and, later, when defeated by the Dutch, underwent extensive additions to it's fortifications from 1649  onwards, until captured by the British in 1796. Today it is a UNESCO site and the Dutch influence on the architecture of the area is clearly evident. Some of the building that still exist include  the Dutch Reformed Church, Government House,  National Maritime Museum, Old Dutch Hospital and, of course, the fortified walls and bastions of the town, A good guide will point our the few landmarks from the Portuguese and the later British occupations. The beginning of the fort’s history, which was built by the Portuguese, along with a Franciscan chapel (now mostly in ruins) inside the fort started  in 1541. 100 years later the Dutch, with a force of some 2,500 men under Koster, captured the fort from the Portuguese in 1640. They started building the fort as seen in its present form in the Dutch architectural style. Fortifications were added up to the early 18th century. The British took over the fort on 23 February 1796, one week after Colombo was captured. Sri Lanka remained a British colony formally from 1815 till it became an independent island nation in 1948. The importance of Galle also declined after the British developed Colombo as their capital and main port in the mid nineteenth century. Today the Sri Lankan government and many Dutch people who still own some of the properties inside the fort are looking at making this one of the modern wonders of the world!  This work is going on still very slowly, I guess there is not enough money yet to build up the Fort to this modern wonder. Maybe the next generation!?

The Fort area is avery large land mass (not indoors) and could potentially take all day to see, if you are walking at a leisurely pace.  I recommend seeing it more than one day in order to spend time relaxing and taking in all of the majestic, panoramic views.  An added bonus is the Galle Cricket Club is directly across the street and you get these amazing views of cricket practice and games....at no additional cost. Tuk Tuks are plentiful in this area and their prices are extremely reasonable.  Lots of great variety in cuisine at reasonable/low prices.  I even stopped to have the most delicious scope of pineapple gelato on my walk around.  There is an ATM in the area at the centrally located round-about (it's bit harder to find an ATM for Union Pay, but if you leave the Fort area and head less the 600 meters across the street, you will find banks that take Union Pay). All in all, a great place to hang out.

The Portuguese started it, fortified by the Dutch and last held by the Brits.  The result is a small city, still populated and lived in by locals hosting us tourists within its fortified walls.  The hotels within are beautiful, the narrow alleys and streets full of good food, quality shopping abounds and there is plentiful art all around. One can stroll ALL the streets in a day, while stopping everywhere you find interesting.  And believe me do stop, as you will find some gems (figuratively and literally). Walk the wall at sunset, being sure to find yourself on the southwest side before dusk, or you may find yourself without a seat.  All the locals will be out, flying kites, taking wedding pics and admiring the sunset with you.  It's quite the people and sunset watching scene.  Lastly wear comfy shoes.

The Dutch Fort of Galle in Southern Sri Lanka is a World Heritage site with many great attractions. For me, the greatest attraction is the Fort Wall (Ramparts) and the fascinating Indian Ocean below and beyond it! Apart from this there are architectural marvels such as the old Dutch hospital, numerous houses, government buildings etc dating back to the same era. The light house is a major attraction, too. Many of the houses and other small buildings are now converted to the numerous shops and restaurants, of course, without harming the original architecture and the theme. This place is immensely popular among the international tourists for obvious reasons. I would not hesitate to state that Galle Fort alone is an adequate reason for someone with a taste for historical places to pay a visit to the island nation Sri Lanka. There's something for everyone in the family here. Kids can play in the beautiful sloping grassland. Teenagers can play a game of cricket if they know how to play the game. They can also take long strolls up and down the sloping walkways on the ramparts and spend quality time. Young adults can jog along the long tracks. However, in my opinion, just sitting and gazing at the immense Indian Ocean from a good vantage point on the ramparts is a superb way to spend quality time as well. Early morning and evening are the best times to be here. Perhaps, one should do a morning round and then return in the evening as well. Moonlit evenings here would make you wonder if you are on earth or in heaven! If you get hungry anytime, there are some fantastic restaurants to help you. The old Dutch hospital which is now converted to a shopping area has several great restaurants such as Minute by Tuk Tuk upstairs. If you sit at the seaside corner you can enjoy amazing views of the ocean while enjoying a delicious meal. There are many resorts and homestays inside the Fort that provides decent accommodation. The narrow streets on the land side of the Fort (opposite the ramparts) has many interesting shops selling various stuff, mainly handicrafts, gems etc. There are some great restaurants and ice cream vendors as well along these alleyways. Be mindful when you walk on these roads as people, bicycles, motor cycles, trishaws and vehicles have to share the same road. However, unlike in many other parts of Sri Lanka, co-existence seems to work very well here. If you have a choice visit the Galle Fort during the time of world famous Galle Literary Festival. Though there will be so much congestion and people touching shoulders you will not regret as evening to night there is so much happening including cultural shows under mesmerizing displays lighting etc. You would feel as if the whole world is here in Galle with tourists from all over the world gathering at Galle Fort during this time.

We can imagine attackers trying to breach the magnificent thick sloping walls, lookouts in lonely bartizans, and responses of defenders.  The old Portuguese Galle fort, built mostly of palm trees and mud, and later extended, was conquered by the Dutch in 1640 who brought their cannon to higher ground and aimed fire into the fort.  The most dramatic ramparts of the stronger and newer stone and coral Dutch/British-built fort are on the ocean side, but there is no record of their fort being attacked from sea, or from land, and even the 2004 tsunami did not breach it.   A better-restored fort and environs with changing of the guard, old cannon, Sunday night fireworks, and authentic chambers would offer an opportunity to attract more paying visitors.  But now visitors can enter free and still get an idea of the size of the Dutch/British fort at its height in the 1850s before the British center of influence gravitated from Galle to Colombo.  Our favorite walks around the fort are on the two levels facing the sea and atop the wall leading to the lighthouse.

Every visitor to Galle should make Galle Fort their first stop. It is a vibrant place and where many of Galle’s best shops and restaurants are. The place is buzzing. According to Ptolemy’s per his world map of 125-150 AD, Galle was already a busy port, trading with China, Greece and the Arab countries. Some historians believe that Galle is the Tarshish of biblical times and is where King Solomon traded for gemstones, spices and peacocks. It is certainly possible but there is no evidence to support the belief. What is known is that Galle is where the Portuguese first landed in 1505 after having been blown off course on their way to The Maldives. The original fort, built as a palisade of palm trees and mud, by the Portuguese in 1588, to enforce colonial rule and keep out the natives, was later extended to include a watch tower and 3 bastions to ward off potential attacks from the land side by the native Sinhalese. During the Portuguese occupation the fort contained a prison camp for the Sinhalese. The old fort, considered structurally insecure, was demolished by the Dutch who, after ousting the Portuguese in 1640, replaced it with their own, much bigger and secure fort, covering 36 hectares encircling the entire rocky peninsular, between 1649 and 1663. Within the protective massive stone walls the Dutch constructed administration buildings, a church, warehouses, arsenal, gun house, workshops and housing, including the Commandant’s residence. An elaborate sewerage system, that flooded at high tide, was also constructed by the Dutch to drain the sewage. Before the development of Colombo as the commercial centre of Ceylon, Galle was the major port and trading centre of the country for over 200  years. When the British replaced the Dutch in 1796, Galle had already become a relative backwater, having already been supplanted by Colombo as the capital and major port. As the British further developed Colombo, the streets and ancient buildings within the Galle Fort area, were allowed to deteriorate as Galle’s influence declined. The original lighthouse was built during the British time. That burnt down in a fire in 1936 and the rebuilt lighthouse dates from 1938. The historic importance of the Fort area (Old Galle) with its narrow streets and old Portuguese and Dutch colonial buildings, was recognized and in 1988 Galle Fort was granted World Heritage Site status by UNESCO. The Government of Sri Lanka, through its Galle Heritage Foundation under the Ministry of Cultural Affairs and National Heritage has taken the initiative of restoring some of the heritage buildings to their old glory. The restoration work, conforming to the guidelines provided by the University of Moratuwa, has been financially supported by the Government of the Netherlands. Like much of Galle town, the old fort suffered some damage in the 2004 tsunami but the fortifications and the many damaged houses were repaired to the original colonial style under the direction of the Ministry of Cultural Affairs. During the civil war that lasted 26 years there was little change in Galle, as the tourists stayed away, but after the civil war ended in 2008, tourists began to return and for them a popular destination was Galle Fort. As a direct result many of the existing buildings here were bought up by expatriates and wealthy Sri Lankans, renovated and converted to bijou restaurants, fine houses, hotels, boutiques, bars and smart shops. The fort area is now home to many artists, writers, photographers, designers and poets of foreign origin but more than half of the population are moors. There is a visitor centre and more information about the fort and its history can be found at the museums. Things to do at the fort usually involve strolling, either around the ramparts, or along the narrow streets or just browsing in the exclusive shops. New smart shops are appearing almost by the month. When you tire of strolling and browsing you can stop for a welcome cup of coffee or ice cream or a good meal. There are also 2 museums where you can escape from the sun. Also, on your strolls, keep your eyes open for Galle Fort’s symbol, the cockerel, usually carved in stone, and recorded in various places including over the main entrance gate. It is thought that the name Galle is derived from the Portuguese word for cockerel – galo because when the Portuguese first landed in 1505 they heard the crowing of a cockerel. An alternative derivation for the name Galle is that the Sinhala name for rock is gala. I think the latter is the more likely but the former explanation is the more interesting. Or maybe it’s a happy combination of both. On Saturdays there is a small, but select, craft market. In January Galle hosts the Fairway Galle Literary Festival. It is primarily a book festival with world celebrity authors visiting, but the old Galle Fort also comes alive with music ranging from jazz to choral, wine and whisky tasting, guided walking tours, gourmet food and parties or just for people watching. It is a very good time to visit Galle, but you need to reserve accommodation well in advance because later the prices usually rise to meet demand. [Background info from Wikipedia]

Galle was a major port in Sri Lanka and still handles shipping and cruising yachts. The Dutch Museum, Groote Kerk (Great Church) and the National Maritime Museum are some of the famous tourist attractions in Galle. The city is also famous for its delicate handmade lace and ebony carvings. The Galle International Cricket Stadium has also contributed to enhance the image of the city as a sports destination.

It sits on a peninsular, past Galles' old harbour and provides a commending view of the area and must have been a very impressive structure in its day. One of my main interests was to see the Cricket ground, which is adjacent to the fort, where England play their Test Matches, when touring Sri Lanka. This of course, plus the whole area was badly damaged by the Tsunami of 2004 and it was good to see the efforts made to renovate the area after the extensive damage caused. Founded by the Portuguese in the 17th century, taken Over and built out to its current form by the Dutch in the mid 17th century and finally occupied by the British from late 18th till independence in mid 20th century, this fort oozes colonial charm. Seemingly full of foreigners who have taken over and renovated the historical houses and buildings now full of restaurants, quaint hotels and interesting shops with antiques and curiosa, it’s fun to to just wander around and soak in the atmosphere. The seawalls are in a superb state considering the pounding they’d get each year with the storms. You can walk on them all around the peninsula area. I love the frangipani trees everywhere that provide shade to the local merchants for selling their wares.

You can walk all the way almost around the city of Galle. A great part is accessible, but not always for disabled persons. Especially at sunsettime you can enjoy the beautiful views. During the day it is worth walking around too, because most of the historical buildings are to be seen from the ramparts. The lighthouse is a good sign to know where you are. Because there are so many people in the evening, enjoying the same views, it is very safe to walk around.

Galle Fort is much bigger than we thought; it took us a good couple of hours of gentle strolling to walk all around the perimter to the lighthouse – the only one on Sri Lanka, and quite underwhelming.  Although interesting to poke around, there is nothing to indicate what you're actually seeing and walking on. There is a map and a legend on a board outside the fort, but it's impossible to remember any details.  If you want to know the history, you'll find loads of information by doing a Google search; this will not mention the rubbish and the (courting?) couples lurking in dark corners. The old town of Galle is quite picturesque, crammed as it is with quaint shops selling mainly trendy clothes, atrifacts and gems. The gem dealers are really pushy – as soon as you breathe on a shop window you'll suddenly feel the presence of a dealer – usually a smiling man, rubbing his hands – urging you inside to “have a look, no obligation”.  There are many assorted cafes and restaurants offering a variety of food from local to international.  You'll also spot some very old European cars: Morris 1000, minis and VW Beetles, some being used as props for what look like “spontaneous” wedding photos. The quiet part of the old town – round by the court houses and old hospital – are worth a stroll, and if you wander through the entrance towards the Naval Museum and out onto the dock you might catch a glimps of the monkeys – I think they're a type of langur – high in the trees. You'll also see the most amazing tree by the courthouses. All in all there is really very little to recommend this town – it's a pleasant enough place to wander for half a day or so, but nothing spectacular, just another tourist trap.

Galle is a major city in Sri Lanka, situated on the southwestern tip.It was known as Gimhathitha in ancient times before the arrival of the Portuguese in the 16th century, when it was the main port on the island.The city was extensively fortified by the Dutch during the 17th century from 1649 - 1663. They built a fortified solid granite wall and three bastions, known as "Sun", "Moon" and "Star". Galle is the best example of a fortified city built by the Portuguese in South and Southeast Asia, showing the interaction between Portuguese architectural styles and native traditions. In 1640, the Portuguese were forced to surrender to the Dutch East India Company. The Galle fort is a world heritage site and is the largest remaining fortress in Asia built by European occupiers. Prominent landmarks in Galle include the one of the main Shiva temples on the island, the city's natural harbor, St. Mary's Cathedral founded by Jesuit Priests & the National Maritime Museum. So the second time in Sri Lanka before my trip finished in Tangalle beach, we decided to visit Galle and stay for 4 nights. I had the opinion as a very touristic place, evening would also be like the morning full of the tourists that it would have a lot of fuss (Like all the touristic place, like Santorini, where I live and work.). But for my surprise, between 20:00 to 21:00 o'clock all the shops including restaurants cafes etc. was closed. That means the Fort at night was very quiet and you can enjoy the Fort in tranquility it was fabulous. You have many things to do besides your tour of the Galle Fort, small getaways in the around area, visit visit different beaches etc. For Sure in my next trip to Sri Lanka I visit again Galle Fort.

Fort Galle in an incredible place that will charm you with its colonial look and rich history. Galle is an ancient port in Sri Lanka that during the European expansion was, first, the base for Portugese tradesmen who build a tiny stronghold, then Holland overtook the place and build a regular fort, which was later conquered by the English colonisers. Thankfully, the English left the fort as it was and today the place is full of wonderful architecture. The fort is located on a small peninsula and it's closed within medieval walls, so once you're there, you can enjoy a wall on the actual fortification wall. All in all, Fort Galle is a testament to a very charged history and experiencing this gem is worth your while.

Galle Fort, in the Bay of Galle on the southwest coast of Sri Lanka, was built first in 1588 by the Portuguese, then extensively fortified by the Dutch during the 17th century from 1649 onwards. ... The fort has a colourful history, and today has a multi-ethnic and multi-religious population. Built‎: ‎1584 and 1684 Built by‎: ‎Portuguese and ‎dutch Battles/wars‎: ‎siege of galle 1640; Several other battles Materials‎ ‎granite‎ ‎stones and coral Today's town has grown greatly and spreads into the surroundings but the Fort is the slowbeating heart of Galle's history. The walled city Cladius Ptolomy's 1st century map of the world clearly shows Traprobana (Sri Lanka) off the coast of India. Because of the island's importance as a center for ancient trade between East and West it was thought to be much larger than we know it to be today. Galle is not named but its harbor is depicted on the map. The map reference of Hodora may refer to the modern place name of Dondra which is just south of Galle. Cosmas Indicopleustes, an Egyptian monk, in his 545 AD work Christian Topography writes "This same Sielediba [Sri Lanka] then, placed as one may say, in the center of the Indies and possessing the hyacinth receives imports from all the seats of commerce and in turn exports to them, and is thus itself a great seat of commerce." The place 'Hyacinth' referred to is believed to be Galle. Ibn Battuta a Moroccan explorer visited Galle which he called Quli in 1344 he found it to be a bustling port. The grand treasury fleet of the Chinese admiral Zheng He made four visits to the port of Galle between 1406 and 1433 (The galle national meseum as has a scale model of these gigantic ships and a comparable European ship of the time which is dwarfed by these ancient Chinese juggernauts). A copy of the trilingual inscription left by him at Galle in 1411 can also be seen at the museum.

Galle Fort Originally built by Portuguese traders the Fort has seen a succession of occupying forces. Originally the Portuguese only occupied the coastal areas protected by a string of forts of which Galle was the biggest and best defended. It was also the main port in Sri Lanka until The rise of Colombo. Then along came the Dutch who ousted the Portuguese throughout Sri Lanka adding to the fortifications. Within the ramparts is a beautifully preserved Dutch Orthodox Church within which can be seen numerous old grave markers from as far back as the early 1700's. The Dutch were followed by the English who not only occupied the forts but colonised the whole island bringing with them law and administration much of which is still embedded within the Sri Lankan constitution. The Fort itself withstood the full force of the Sunami but much of the surrounding town was severely damaged with a huge lose of life. Those within were safe. It is possible to tour the outer ring Road inside the ramparts in a car or bus, but it is much better to explore the central narrow streets on foot were you will find many small souvenir shops, small hotels, and cafes. We have always found the prices here to be reasonable, but a bit of bartering is always fun. We has lunch t Pedlars Corner Cafe, which I have reviewed separately.

Tuesday 6th October, we took the bus from our Hotel in Ahungalla, Riu Sri Lanka, to Galle. The bus journey took  about 1 hour and cost 60 Rupees each (about 30p). The Fort is  situated on the South West Coast of Sri Lanka. It has a long history, it was first built in 1588 by the Portuguese. Further fortification was undertaken by the Dutch during the 17th century. The British took over the Fort in 1796 till 1948. It has been designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Fort houses the old Town of Galle and is sometimes referred to as the Dutch Fort or the Ramparts of Galle. It also withstood the ravages of the Tsunami in December 2004. It is well worth combining a walk around the Old Town (reviewed separately) and the ramparts of the amazing old structure.

Any visitor to Galle Fort must buy this wonderful little book, "Galle Fort World Heritage Site – A Visitor’s Guide and Illustrated Walking Tour by Mark Thompson and Karl Steinberg". Without a doubt, it is the most practical, useful guide I have purchased, and it made my first visit to this place a much richer experience than it would otherwise have been. A fold out map at the back of the guide details an achievable walk around the Fort’s most significant buildings, with numbered signposts for each of these. Details about the buildings’ history can be found in the chapters whose numbers correspond to those on the map. The book is well written – easy to read, informative and entertaining. Beautiful, varied illustrations (photographs, maps, art works) accompany the text and add further enjoyment. We spent half a day on this walking tour, but that included a stop for morning tea, lunch, and a bit of shopping. I bought the book at Barefoot but, when I went to buy another copy, was surprised to find that it wasn’t widely available. However, it is definitely worth searching out.

We are a family of 5 and we spent a few hours wandering around this impressive fort with plenty of old colonial buildings inside. Fantastic views. We got there about 3.30pm which was probably s little too early as it was very hot.

So we arrived in the rain. On the way here we had passed the usual tiny shops and the huge scrap yards. The journey on the motorway was lovely... then we were here. Galle came upon us all of a sudden and it really was like we left Sri Lanka behind and stepped into a European city. The French, Dutch and British influences are very strong and give the whole place an almost Portuguese feel. The walls around the sea, the old buildings, land marks and places of worship... none of it feels like it has anything in common with Colombo, Arugambay, Kandy or Ella. It really is alien. Here there is a modern cafe culture, posh hotels at reasonable prices featuring luxuries like towels, hot showers, toilet roll, sheets AND blankets... matching uniforms and so on. Visitors walk around with boutique shopping bags and it is all very surreal. Nowhere did we see piles of rubbish and leaves being burnt at dusk. The police cycle the streets and smile warmly. The tuktuk drivers are polite and not pushy (this is the wrong town for tuktuks as everything is in walking distance). Even the street peddlers are polite. I'm glad we didn't come here first. This just doesn't feel right. When the capital is such a mess how on Earth does a place like this exist? When children learn in a school with no walls, holes in the ceiling and no science equipment how can a little piece of Europe live on like this? My wife called it the St Ives of Sri Lanka and that about sums it up. We were going to skip Galle and I'm so glad we didn't. It is amazing but it isn't the Sri Lanka I've come to know.

The name Galle is synonymous with the attractive Dutch fort, is a tropical paradise that blends in a rich heritage and immense religious value.  Due to its vibrant history and ethnic significance, UNESCO declared Galle, the capital of Southern Sri Lanka, a World Heritage Site. Prior to the arrival of the Portuguese, Galle was known as Gimhathiththa. During the early 16th century when it was under Portuguese rile, Galle was transformed into a significant port. Following the occupation of the Dutch up until the invasion of the British, Galle reached a noteworthy amount of development with its peak mostly occurring during the 18th century. Although major developments took place during foreign rule, Galle was an eminent seaport in prehistoric times as it is documented that valuable spices were traded through the port of Galle. Rich civilisations such as Arabs, Indians, Greeks, Persians and Romans used this port as a major business hub in South Asia. The city of Galle which is 119 kilometres away from Sri Lanka’s commercial centre Colombo, is home to about 100,000 people. This remarkable coastal city has a well established rail road system and it is linked by rail to Colombo and Matara. The exciting beach of Unawatuna is positioned a mere 6 kilometres southeast from the city of Galle.  During October and April many tourists arrive in the country just to experience and explore the enthralling beach life of this splendid city. With many attractions located in and around Galle, visitors are sure to enjoy the rich cultural amd historical valued of the city. Attractions such as the Galle Fort, The Maritime Museum and famous Galle lighthouse are some of the many sights within this city. The Galle International Cricket Stadium that holds several international as well as national matches is one of the most recent additions to the historical city of Galle. Galle is a perfect example of the fusion of European and Asian styles. Its natural beauty, superb archaeological location and rich heritage have made it an outstanding coastal city of Sri Lanka.

We left the Kingsbury hotel in Colombo just after 09.00 and arrived in Galle some three hours plus later.  The drive paralleled the Indian Ocean which offers a superb unspoiled beachfront for mile after mile, virtually the whole way.  We passed through several towns, one of which our driver told us was where the first Muslims had landed in Sri Lanka. Our first stop was outside the Dutch Fort at the place where the Portuguese had built a track to the waterfront to service the Fort.  Locals were swimming here in a small bay, which also had a few boats in a marina.  There was also a Western man fishing off the jetty, not very successfully, having only caught a few small sprat sized fish. Our driver told us that the Fort occupied 97 acres and the buildings within the perimeter wall were largely frozen in time.  The styles and usage reflected the different periods of occupation from the Portuguese, Dutch and English. The Dutch Protestant church sits next to an imposing three-storey building originally built for the Dutch governor in 1684. In 1865 the British converted it into a barracks and later into the famous New Oriental Hotel, now called the Amangalla Hotel. The area next to the walls were divided into batteries, each named so that the Commander could deploy forces and parade his troops.  Brighton battery on which we walked is partly grassed over and overlooks the Indian Ocean with sweeping views for miles along the coast. We were surprised at the good state of everything within the Fort and the cleanliness, and regret that we had insufficient time to explore in more detail. Driving through Galle itself, many of the roads have now been made into a one-way system, due to the narrowness of the streets and the amount of traffic.  Small shops predominated and there was a general air of bustling activity.

With no admission fee and so much to see in the "huge area" inside the walls and also being in such close proximity to the Galle train station (just across the road from the station & a few minutes' walk, in fact you can see the Fort's wall on the north side & the Clock Tower from right outside the train station), this fort should be a definite "must" for every tourist to Sri Lanka. I started inside by going above the wall on the entrance side (north side) where I checked out the Clock Tower (and also the green life-sized figures of Dutch soldiers guarding the Fort and those of some locals which you might miss if you're in a hurry, but they're just on the right side of the ramp leading to the Clock Tower from the ground below) and then just continued along the path above to the west side (which would be the right side if you're looking at the Fort from outside and which has the "longest stretch" of wall among the four sides) where you can totally take in wide-open views of the sea especially from these bastion lookout areas jutting out into the sea (you can actually go down the steps from one of them to the "tiny" beach below where I saw some local people swimming, and yes also the water immediately around the Fort is quite shallow which I guess makes it "ideal" for bathing although I only saw locals and not tourists doing that).  Above the wall finally came to an end at the Lighthouse on the corner of the south side (the far side from the entrance) & the east side where you'll also see the white temple on the mountain called Rumasallah at some distance to the east across the water. On the grounds (this fort, by the way, is an actual "living area" and not just a big open area for display purposes like you see in some countries) are places to stop by like the beautiful white mosque near the Lighthouse, the big yellow Maritime Museum, the Black Fort, something like three churches and a Buddhist temple, but I found many of them "inaccessible" due to their day of closure (like the Maritime Museum) or due to renovation (like the Black Fort); only went into two churches, one of them being the oldest church in Galle called Dutch Reformed Church with "memorial plates" similar to tomb plates on its grounds, which were both "pretty plain" inside (nothing like churches of Old Goa in India with "elaborate" interiors!) followed by the small Buddhist temple (closer to the west side, you can actually see it while walking along the wall on that side) with a "fairly big" reclining Buddha inside. It's only about a two-and-a-half-hour train ride from Colombo along the coastal route; and if you're paying attention to the scenery, you'll see at certain times the train is going "almost as if" right on top of the rocks bordering land and sea!  The only downside about the Sri Lankan trains (maybe it was because of the time of the Sri Lankan New Year) was I bought tickets for Class 2 and found the Class 2 seats all occupied both for this trip and the one to Habarana (for going to the Sigiriya Lion Rock); the only chance of getting a seat in the right class (that you pay for) seemed only if you were to board at the "end-of-line" stations like Colombo Fort or Batticaloa or Trincomalee (don't know what's the end station for the line to Galle, but it's not Galle!), and there was not even a conductor on the train to check the tickets which "clearly" made it possible for like Class 3 people riding in Class 2!!

utch Fort at Galle, close to the island’s southernmost point, 173km from Colombo, has the distinction of being the best-preserved sea fort in South Asia. A living heritage site, this 90 hectare (222 acre) attraction is a superb blend of architecture, with fortifications that resemble those in the coastal areas of Portugal. The fall of Galle to the Dutch in 1640 saw its fortifications consolidated further along the lines of the fortified cities of Europe. The Dutch and the English colonial styles are evident in the deep verandahs of houses supported by timber or masonry pillars. Originally established by the Portuguese in the 16th Century, it reached its zenith under Dutch rule in the 18th Century, providing spacious housing, wide roads and all necessary facilities within its walls including an intricate sewage system that was ahead of its time. When it comes to fortified towns, nothing can compete with the Dutch Fort in Galle. This World Heritage Site on the south coast was the main port of call for ships sailing between the East and Europe. Today, inside the Fort you will find that it exudes old-world charm. Within the ramparts and stonewalls of the old Galle Fort – which spreads over a 36-hectare peninsula — magnificent buildings remain. The narrow streets are dotted with Dutch colonial villas and there's a welcome absence of vehicular traffic. There are several museums and antique shops that display curiosities from the island's colonial era. Of the many colonial buildings, perhaps the most absorbing is the Dutch Reformed Church, containing ornately carved memorials to the city's Dutch settlers. The original entrance gate to the Fort, on the northeast side of the peninsula still bears the carved insignia of the Dutch East Indies Company (or VOC, from “Vereenigde Oost Indische Compagnie”). The Fort also hosts some of the island's most exclusive boutique-style accommodation in former villas restored to their colonial glory.

Listed as a UNESCO heritage attraction, Galle Fort is one of the must visit places during your visit to Sri Lanka. It overlooks the famous Galle international cricket ground, with its own special history, and the beautiful ocean.  Inside, you can see a lot of historical Dutch buildings and restaurants and people of all tricks and trades. The Sri Lankan army cricket team were playing cricket in the nets and they were happy for me to join in for a quick few sixes off my bowling. There were two snake charmers very happy to show off their snakes, a python and a non-venomous cobra, or so he re-assured me. They also have to monkeys, similar to those in Aladdin, but I wouldn't go too close to them, since one actually bit their little girl. Otherwise, there are coin dealers and boat craft sellers. I would just stay wise with all these crafty guys. The Dutch Reformed church and other Dutch buildings are worth a quick visit for history buffs. The fort is also popular for wedding photos for obvious reasons. There are restaurants and an ATM for those who can't pay with coconuts. And if you're a Mario nerd, you obviously have to save queeny. Go try your luck at a gentleman's game.

Wandering around and losing myself in old streets, gazing at people and up at windows, or balconies full of blooms, admiring the old houses and imagining how people lived back then has always been something I have enjoyed. The beauty of Galle Fort is that it is a living fort. The old homes are alive with the current generation of ancient families.Each of them has a story to tell or something to share, not just a trinket store or restaurant. The souvenir and art shops, the cafes and the old houses, museums, churches, court house, the hospital, gracious hotels, the lighthouse, antique stores, chichi boutiques, jewellery stores and ice cream shops are all charming and quaint. I spent three days wandering around, taking photos, writing post cards and sending them off at the old post office and I went to the local museums, watched the sunset at the ligh house, ate hand churned ice cream, watched families swim in the blue bay, shopped at some beautiful stores, peered into old homes and found serendipity. I was happy to visit and speak with the Pastor at the Church, and learn its history. We had an enjoyable, if touristy, dinner at the restored Dutch Hospital. Galle Fort, in the harbour of Galle in south west Sri Lanka is a wonderful place to visit to gain a sense of history of the nation and to enjoy its fascinating buildings. The Fort was constructed by the Portuguese in the 16th century and later fortified by the Dutch. It has an absolutely fascinating array of buildings in varying styles, small winding streets with art and souvenir shops and a substantial number of hotels and restaurants of varying prices. The Fort area has a peaceful atmosphere away from the busy Galle town, but is very busy with tourists. An early morning visit is ideal. Views from the outer walls are wonderful. It is a lovely place to spend half a day or more strolling about and enjoying its very varied attractions and views.

Galle is one of the famous ancient harbours in Sri Lanka and it became very famous during Portuguese and Dutch periods. Now you can see Dutch Fort that built by Dutch 17th century. It is a World Heritage Site. Dutch colonial buildings, church, rampart, 12 bastions, old VOC company monogram etc. can be seen.

Once you're inside, start exploring it on foot, as this is a great place to take a stroll. Though I must warn you it is darn hot out there. You will be sweating like a pig, I guarantee it. They say everything's more expensive inside the fort, and it probably is true. But it's just that much more atmospheric. It's worth it, I say. Have fun out there.

My daughter and I spent a couple of days in Galle Fort early in January 2015. We loved it. There are many little restaurants tucked into side streets alongside little shops. There was live entertainment in the evenings near the wall overlooking the ocean and beach. The storekeepers are friendly and there are many foreigners from many different lands walking up and down the lit streets day and night. We ventured outside the fort to get some information from the tourist board and learned a lot about the area, too. We were looking to rent motorcycles (not scooters), and the tourism clerk matched us up with a driver of a metered tuk-tuk by the name of Pradeep Sugath to take us to a nearby town where he thought we'd find some rentals. We had not known about metered tuk-tuks until the clerk explained that the government employs a number of tuk-tuk drivers who charge only 80 rupees per km. This was big news to us! We had been bargaining with tuk-tuk drivers for five days already, and it always seemed drivers wanted to charge at least 100rp per km. We wish we had known about the metered tuk-tuks from Day 1! Pradeep took us to several motorcycle rental places so we could get the best deal, then he took us to the market and showed us where we could get the best tea. After that, he took us to the Unawatuna Dive Centre, where we had arranged for an afternoon of Scuba Diving. We calculated the difference between the beginning odometer reading and the end, and multiplied by 80rp and paid that amount. Very straightforward. I asked Pradeep why he prefered to drive a metered tuk-tuk and he replied that he felt the private tuk-tuk drivers were always seeing tourists as "targets for money." He prefers not to get caught up in the bargaining and the selling of his services and concentrate more on helping visitors find what they want and need, which he did really well for us. He drives the tuk-tuk part-time and gives car tours all over Sri Lanka when he's not driving the tuk-tuk in and around Galle. We would definitely have booked a car tour with him if our flight out wasn't scheduled for the next day. We would have gotten an "insider's" perspective on the country, the politics (the election was scheduled to take place 3 days after our departure), and the culture. If you want to arrange for your own tour, Pradeep has a gmail account under his name: pradeephsugath  He was unlike any other driver we met in all the time we were in Sri Lanka - very respectful, honest, kind, curious, and generous.

It's only recently that I started exploring the inner fort, the lovely streets, and pieces of architecture including the church, mosque and the dutch flavored houses. While we don't cherish a century long dutch rule, what they left behind - especially the glorious and long lasting architecture is priceless. Walk down those narrow streets inside the fort, where dutch architectural houses-turned-into street shops, restaurants and boutiques, provide a beautiful picture. You feel like you are in different part of the world. It seems everything inside the fort is tourists oriented, and a bit expensive - even the few restaurants inside. Enjoyed walking on the streets looking at the impressive buildings, visiting interesting places like the Maritime museum, the Dutch Reform Church, Library and the Post Office (the latter is unfortunately in a terrible state but deserves to be rescued) and the interesting personal museum that belongs to an entrepreneur/fort resident. Coming from a country that's awash with history and castles, walls, etc, Including a World famous castle that goes back at least a thousand years and the Roman walls of Antonine and Hadrian going back even further, oh yes it was going to take a lot to impress me here. Unfortunately I wasn't, as when I entered and saw the many overpriced shops, B&B's and the  streets along with the customary beggars, my heart sank as I realised this was just another tourist trap. However, the only thing I saw of any interest were the views and the restaurants which were actually pretty good, slightly expensive but, clean and serving some decent grub along with the obligatory cold beers. And the banks with the ever handy ATM's. Now, as one reviewer from Dubai has stated below, the ramparts surrounding this mini town were in a real state of disrepair and it was obvious no one gave a toss about them now. Walking around one could see the graffiti, litter, cheap repairs, grass growing everywhere, a real shame indeed. There are even signs going by the smell that people are using certain parts as toilets as there are none nearby. I would also recommend you avoid the snake charmers as I suspect their snakes are probably de-fanged in the most horrific way imaginable to "entertain" tourists, and they do have a short life expectancy.  Even more alarming was to come here and as we were standing at the old flag pole end admiring the views, a group of young lads came up and one  lad asked me if I wanted to see him dive off the ramparts and into the sea below for a fee. Looking down at the waves crashing against the rocks, I quickly informed him quite angrily that there was no way I would pay him to do that and this lad possibly ending up in a wheelchair for the rest of his life for a few Rupees, he just smiled and moved onto the next gullible tourist. I know life's cheap here but, just be warned as you could have this on your conscience, not quite a holiday souvenir to take home.? The plus side of this walled town was the nice walk along the ramparts and the views to behold just watch the sun too as it gets pretty hot, there are also plenty of vendors selling cold drinks/snacks etc as well as the hawkers selling their tat , and if your looking for any bargains in the shops here? Forget it, as they are mostly jewellery and very expensive, even the small souvenir shops were taking the mickey. You'll find a couple of places of interest like the maritime museum and some old churches to explore but, that's about that I'm afraid and on a footnote the famous old walls did prevent the boxing day Tsunami of 2004 from penetrating the town probably saving hundreds of lives that morning and still withstanding the test of time it would seem. ? The Galle fort is probably well worth a visit these days if only to spend a day out, just don't expect too much...!

Rumassala, known to colonialists as Buona Vista, is the subject of many legends. It features in the Ramayana, as the home of the beautiful queen Sita, hidden in the jungle nearby. Hanuman who was sent to fetch a medicinal plant for a wounded soldier, was unable to find it and brought the Himalayan mountains on which it was said to grow. He dropped a chunk at Unawatuna ('here it fell') to form the present mountain, where many medicinal plants still grow. There is a major magnetic anomaly near Unawatuna, which Arthur C. Clarke attributes to a meteorite strike, and it is said that satellites lose their orbits with unusual frequency overhead. The Portuguese had a dreadful reputation in Sri Lanka as looters and pirates, and are said to have given false light signals from Rumassala to lure unsuspecting Arab trading ships onto the rocks

Like most reasonable people I planned a holiday to Sri Lanka to take a break and to enjoy the sun and the sand and boy was I in for a surprise What was meant to be a warm, sunny getaway turned out to be a wet, pouring journey from Airport in Colombo to the quaint little city of Galle And mind you one is not cribbing at all but is amazed by how when you let Life happen to you instead of trying to control every single aspect of it, you will be given much more than your expectations and that’s exactly what happened to me on my Galle Trip The freshness of the air hits you the moment you step out from your cab in Galle and I guess the ‘smog infested’ lungs of Mumbai dwellers go on a natural high thanks to the crisp morning air and the smile comes and stays for a while I has planned a trip alone to Galle and this was a first of sorts and also this was unplanned and other than landing at my friend’s house, there literally was no agenda on the platter and that is when an adventure began We reached with finding the doors locked and while we were waiting it was more than clear that we were in an unpredictable tropical country with its fair share of creepy crawly. It’s a surprise I didn’t jump with fright when I saw a regular Sri Lankan mosquito man. Disconcertingly big these things were and let’s not talk about the lizards and other green slimy things So now the stage was set for a hide and seek between unpredictable nature and city dwellers and for once single girl in the city was determined to win the nature war As soon as we kept our luggage, we wanted to hit the Galle Fort which is a must visit for one and all for many reasons .Its majestic to begin with and if you are the ‘walking’ kind then it’s a discovery of many things What’s peculiar about Galle is how the people are very friendly but since no one really knows English, you end up smiling and nodding a lot at each other and it almost seems as if you are bumping into the same people again and again. Point being it’s a really small town and you can quickly cover it If you are walking alone, you will be hawked a lot of local fruit and other delights including the art and the artistes Art and history is everywhere in Galle and just like ‘sada’ India everything is sold as ‘precious and authentic’ and that’s where the fun begins. The art galleries are a delight of local work and it’s a lot of inspired art from the wartime and ‘Art’ is more about hope than anything else in Galle If like me you have an imagination and look for ghost stories and relics than there are lots of churches and old markets which will fulfill your desire for ‘spookiness’. Enter and sit for a while to soak in the flavour of any old place you visit While at the fort don’t miss the clock tower and the light house as the view is beyond your imagination and almost makes you fall in love with the ‘stranger’ sitting on the next rock. Its romantic and smells divine and you have you gola and local eats and also nariyal paani. Two quaint things about Galle is the ‘head gear’ local women sport and the ‘Hand Pankha’.everyone seemed to carry them and you almost felt as if you were back in the 18th century The food is divine mostly of you are a non-vegetarian but for the vegetarians like me you will find a lot of local juicy fruits which they also use to cook vegetables. ’Cucumber Sabzi’ was my favourite While at the fort I also went to ‘Aman Galla’-One of the most expensive and oldish hotel in Galle and even though there were no tourists, one got to see why it was on every travel site list. It was Dutch and colonial and class was seeping from the walls and the last owner ‘Nesta’ was everywhere in essence. It was almost as if the current management was seeking her approval and did not dare change a thing about the erstwhile NOH Hotel. A Must visit and don’t forget to have one drink while at it Like most people I also went to the ‘Peace Pagoda’ but for me it was again the water and the beach next door which was more enticing than the Buddha Story per say. The place beckons to the lonely heart and you feel engulfed and loved and the peace is something I am still carrying with myself Everywhere you turn there was water and the local population and the foreigners mingled seamlessly and there were very few tourists and that was apparent in the travel rates and in lack of freshness of stock to sell The sleepiness of the island town catches you and you feel compelled to slow down to the extent that the frenzy of existence in your life leaves you gasping and you pat yourself for being able to do it all. The island is built to do ‘less’ and not ‘more’ and while on a holiday, that’s almost divine We decided to also visit the hills while in Galle and if you go to any of the Heritage Hotels like Lighthouse or any other ask for things off the menu and if you smile widely enough they will make it and the end result will be finger smacking good And yes when in Sri Lanka don’t forget to pick up the gems for Mum at home. She would love you more and they are pretty and oh so cheap. You almost feel like a princess for being able to afford it all. If you like the ‘Tall, dark’ handsome variety of men then Sri Lanka has lots of eye candy to offer and a holiday romance or two never harmed anyone. Travel on !!

It was a memorable experience walking along the allies of the Galle fort after many years. This time it was with my wife & 2 daughters. I was able to walk safely in most areas except some areas near the lighthouse at night as there were too many party revellers going overboard. My family & I picked up dozens of broken bottles every morning on the beach for 4 days near the light house left by the carefree visitors. The beach was littered with babies drapers, polythene bags, left over food, sanitary napkins, cigarette buts, broken bottles & garbage bags thrown by unknown sources. The local authorities were caught napping with no proper plan to clear the areas,  notice boards or fines for wrong doers. I also noticed too many touts making life miserable for foreign visitors. This is not acceptable in tourism. I expected to see some assistance to shallow water coral divers in the area but none were around. The restaurants in th area were few & hardly any choice.  I heard many tourist ask why they cant experience the original southern Sri Lankan cuisine in the area. The truth is that there is not a single such place & no one has even tried to have it. I was not able to taste any traditional Southern Sri Lankan dishes in the restaurants in the fort. Instead it was loaded with restaurants serving  Indian, Arabic, European food. The visitor needs a memory to take back & not to eat what they eat back at home. That is how they would cherish the memory of being in a place. I also need to advise visitors that they should be careful in choosing souvenirs, curios & so called antiques. Most of them are fake sold by unscrupulous traders. I detected loads of them & the Mafia of the traders were quick to send note that I was not to entertained to their shops. My tips for a good visit is start the day early at 06.00 am with a dip in the sea near the light house up to 7.30 am, have breakfast. Start your tour of the ramparts by 8 am & visit the historical buildings & places of interest up to 11.00 am  take a break in yr room if in a guest house / hotel in the fort until 03.00 pm. Start yr stroll again in the allies & get on to the ramparts by 04.30 pm.  The sea gets rough after 10.30 am. Carry a gallon of water which you can buy at a convenience store in town. The water sold by traders in the fort is double the price & the brands sold cannot be relied on. The police & the military staff in the fort are very helpful & they go the extra mile to assist visitors.

Galle is the main town in Southern Province and apart from its manic shops, streets and bus station it offers a stunning piece of history dating from the 16th Century when the Portuguese Navigators took a foothold in Sri Lanka. The site of the fort is said to date from earlier times and the 15th century Chinese explorer, Admiral Zhang Ye established trading links in the vicinity. The Fort was occupied variously by the Portuguese, Dutch and British, the second people giving their name to the modern fort in which is a beautifully preserved example of the Dutch Reformed Church, the floor of which is covered with gravestones. There is so much to see on the periphery of the fort before you begin to explore the interior with its shops, stalls and eateries that a full day is needed to do it justice. History is to be found just round the next corner. A memorable place indeed.

Galle is my born city and the fort is not a new place to be...but after few years I visited the fort in an evening with my family to see how it looks now and to cherish some wonderful memories of the past, when I was a school boy. Old dutch fort is one of the greatest monuments of Sri Lankan history, although it was built by an European Nation in 18th century. Anyone can see and experience the greats of old architecture, lifestyle and the beautiful sea right below the fortress walls. Things to do: Walk around the fortress wall watching the sea, watch the old light house and the old clock tower, watch sunset, play a ball game in the ramparts, evening snack or dinner at roadside with sea breeze blowing across, sea bath and swimming in the natural pool, visit the Buddhist temple and many more....specially lying down on the fortress wall and watch stars around 7-8 pm at night!!!! Tips to get the best out of your tour: Go in groups of at least 2-3- Its much enjoyable and safer too. Start your tour around 3pm- Watch the old clock tower and the front view of the Galle city where you will see the International cricket stadium right infront of your eyes. Then have a walk through the fort streets watching old craftsmanship and the architecture of Dutch/Portuguese buildings. Then go to the natural pool and have a bath...careful with sea urchins! Then have an evening snack- Plenty of street food corners..Don't worry, it is typhoid free!Just enjoy. Have a walk around the fortress wall. You will never feel tired. Sea breeze will keep your hair busy and the body relaxed. Watch the sunset. Its one of the best places in the whole world to watch the the multicolored glittering sunset...you will never forget it. Take a snap and share with your friends in FB or twitter. Play some cricket or volleyball at the ramparts...you will be warmly welcome by the locals if you care to share your passion and friendship. If you like, can visit the Buddhist temple in the fort and speak with the monks. Then feel free to enjoy a local/international cuisine of your choice at a restaurant or a street food center. Last but the best part of it is to lay down on the fortress wall floor and watch stars...something I just love to do which brings me my old memories...Just do it and see what I mean! Hope this would help you...

Galle Fort, in the Bay of Galle on the southwest coast of Sri Lanka, was built first in 1588 by the Portuguese, then extensively fortified by the Dutch during the 17th century from 1649 onwards. Unbelievably different experience inside the Fort compared to the outside! You still can feel the time that Dutch ruled Sri Lanka (Ceylon) in the 17th century. There are lots of stories those building, houses, churches etc. can tell us about that by gone era. The ancient burial place in the Dutch church, ruins of the old light house, the clock tower, look outs along the wall which were used by the guards for firing cannons at possible enemy ships and the dungeon where the prisoners were kept were the highlights of my visit. Don't forget to see the ancient burial ground of a Muslim saint and the pure water well situated down below the Army high security zone. I heard that Muslims in the area make a pilgrimage to this site every year just prior to their fasting season when the gate is opened by the Army,for only one day! It is a very good idea to find someone who has knowledge about the Fort,because there are no signs or written instructions available for tourists. Even though the Department of Archeology has the control over the conservation of the Galle Fort and it's historical value, it is somewhat sad to see some of the old houses and builidings have been either modified under guise of renovation or transformed in to businesses. Tha main attraction of Galle is the historical "Fort Complex" in side the Walls. Why do I call it a complex is due to the achitechtural placement of all required buildings in one single palce. It is visiblae for any one who carefully study the palce. This fort was placed close to the Railway station. and the court, all houses catagorised to rich, government servents, local authorities, army personals, merchents etc, are being placed seperatly on seperate streets. All the streets were stond layed and all the houses are facing to the street. Old retail outlets are still could recognized by it's location near to the court building. The church, restaurants & Bar, Cart parking area and few administrational buildings were also placed seperatly but within the walking distence to provide the best comfert to the citizens in side the fort. Most wonderfull experience I had was, on a rainy day I had to stand under the big stoned arch at the entrence of the fort. I herd some noise of a water flow and suprisingly there were no any sign of a water flow or no any drain was seen around. It increased my curiosity and when I checked the sound was coming within the stoned arch...! cuase there was a drain system within the stoned wall to remove the water geathered on the face of the wall due to rain.....! I was shocked and I went on top of the wall to check the drain system if it is visible. but there were no any sign of a drain system but I still heard the sound.... Also, when checked closly, you can still see the small, very deep cells in the wall which was used to jailed prisnors. and the well placed guard rooms (Watch huts) are still available on the fort wall, and when you step in to a one, you can feel how carefully the fort was protected. When lookd down from the tall wall, you can realised that it was an un concared obstecle made by great dutch engineers to prevent any unauthirised entry to the fort. This was well proved when Tsunami hit Galle, even the furious waves of Tsunami could not pass through this great walls of Galle Fort. If you happen to be in Galle even for a shorter period I woud like to invite you to take a walk on the face of this gret make and enjoy the incredible view of the ornage sun in the evenings.

Galle (pronounced "Gawl") Fort is worth  a morning or afternoon of your time.  There are some old churches and a maritime museum but the best thing to do is to walk the streets and the walls of the old fort ( perhaps at sun down).  Because Sri Lanka (once known as "Ceylon") was highly prized for its spices such as cloves, the European powers fought to controll it - first the Portugese, then the Spanish, followed by the Dutch and lastly the British.  They left behind a great deal of history and architecture inside the vast ramparts of what is really a fort city.  There are several shops, restaurants, hotels, etc.  within the walls.

The buildings in the fort had alot of character, slighly run down british colonial.  Walking around the outer rim of the fort was interesting too.  You could see both into the fort and the surrounding ocean.  Definitely worth a visit.

At the beginning I thought we have come all the way for nothing but passing the fort's entrance arch I realized it was worthy. Awesome conservation status! Cozy houses and restaurants, and a wonderful view of the Indian Ocean from the granite wall... A UNESCO World Heritage Site and the largest remaining fortress after the European occupation- definitely a must-see!! About 1:30 hours from Bentota and 2:00-2:30 hours from Kalutara The beach near the lighthouse is not that big but if you don't really care to swim with locals, then this is the right place for you.  Lots of guest houses available,too. You interested in antiquary, then you may find lots of offers when walking around. Good luck and enjoy your trip!!!

We enjoyed exploring Galle fort and would highly recommend it as a way to understand colonialism in Sri Lanka. The village is still lived in, but you Can take a leisurely stroll around the fort walls. The views are wonderful. You can also stop at any of the cute little restaurants to eat, there are many little places to buy souvenirs, a few little museum ish places(nothing to write home about) and you will be invited in to a dark dank roofless wreck that is purported to be the school where you will be asked to donate money.  Overall the fort site itself was cute, touristy, but the walk around the walls was fabulous. One side note though. We were a bit disappointed with the scam factor. We were approached by a very nice fellow who wanted to share his sad story of the loss of his family in the tsunami. He went on to say that he has a grandson in the hospital who needs milk. He also wanted to show us a great place to go shopping. We have traveled southeast Asia extensively and are no strangers to touts and scammers, but, for some reason, we really hoped Sri Lanka would be better as it was just getting tourism up and running on a large scale again. Back at our guest house, we were not surprised that ever other tourist who went to Galle met different people all with the same story. Another problem is that each little museum and nook wanted to charge entrance fees and they were all a bit overpriced for what you were seeing

The view of Galle cricket stadium on one side and the beautiful blue sea on the other were breathtaking!!! The walk inside the fort was also great and Lihiniya Gems, a shop inside the fort, offered great gems at super-affordable prices!!! Must visit place......

Fort Galle is a UNESCO World heritage site without the usual crowds and tasteless souvenir shops. It's worth strolling around- the fort is so small you cannot get lost . Worth visiting : enter the dutch church and you will see the tombs of dutch colonialists and their wives , the anglican church was unfortunately closed. They also have any number of schools, a country court, a police station dating from 1927 etc. On the streets you will see a blend of people mainly singhalese and muslim descendants of the moors. For shopping you might want to have a look at the quaint antique stores, or get some inexpensive jewelry or local textiles. Not to be missed :  tea at the Colonial style hotel  Amangalla on main street. Note that while the modern city of Galle was badly hit by the Tsunami in 2004 the fort was spared.

There's some beautiful old architecture inside the walls, few museums, churches and cosy little cafes and restaurants (European style) but beware of the prices, they are very high compering to other places.

This is a gem but will rapidly be developed. Many buildings under repair or hopefully appropriate restoration. The paved lane ways are great for a wander morning and late afternoon. The place has not yet suffered under mass tourism and it still retains the sense of community with schools, religious buildings of three different faiths, courts, and even a small army garrison. Go before it is too late.
